seed_variation.verdict: Only one seed was run, so there is no seed variation to measure.
seed_variation.why: A hosted LLM cannot be seeded: our seeds only reach local random generators, and the provider's sampling (temperature etc.) is fixed for this model. So every run can give different text, and the spread across seeds measures the model's own run-to-run variation. Each seed repeats every API call. Each seed sets Python random, NumPy and torch. PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed to the FIRST seed for the whole run.

predictions.SY0103a: The team held a kick-off meeting to discuss designing a voice-controlled kitchen timer. They agreed it should feature on-device processing with a limited command vocabulary, a wake word, short voice feedback, support for multiple timers, and a single physical backup button. The team established a target retail price of twenty-five euros and a production cost limit of twelve fifty per unit. Before the next functional design meeting in thirty minutes, Tomasz will investigate hardware components, power options, and cost breakdowns; Priya will work on voice commands, feedback, and multiple timers; Ben will research customer preferences, pricing acceptance, and brainstorm wake word names; and Laura will distribute the meeting minutes.
predictions.SY0103b: The team met to discuss the functional design of the voice-activated kitchen device, noting that Tomasz was absent due to illness so cost and power decisions are postponed. Following user research presented by Ben, the team revised their timer plans from three named timers to two numbered timers (timer one and timer two) to avoid recognition issues and user confusion. They also agreed on a loud, escalating alarm, selected Kiko as the working product name pending sound testing, and parked the idea of a digital display until cost numbers are available.
predictions.SY0103c: The team reviewed conceptual design options for their offline voice-controlled kitchen timer, keeping within the twelve euro fifty maximum production cost. They decided on mains power using a USB-C adapter and agreed to include a small two-digit LED display. They confirmed 'Kiko' as the working wake word after discussing minor false triggers and agreed to market the device on its lack of a required app and its offline privacy. Finally, they agreed on a round, wipeable plastic design where the top acts as a large rubber button with the display in the center.
predictions.SY0103d: The team reviewed the detailed design and physical model of the Kiko voice timer. Tomasz reported that the supplier retrained the wake word model for free to eliminate false triggers on the word cocoa. The meeting discussed the physical form, agreeing to add a rubber ring on the bottom to prevent sliding, and approved a white LED display. The display will alternate between two running timers using a decimal point indicator, and the button controls were simplified so a short press stops the alarm and a three-second hold cancels timers. The team selected two final colourways, white with an orange top and charcoal with a lime green top. The unit cost stands at eleven forty, leaving a tight safety margin under the twelve fifty target, and the evaluation confirmed the timer meets all functional and hands-free requirements.
predictions.SY0110a: Priya, Tom, and Jonas held a kickoff meeting for a new reusable coffee cup project with a deposit system, while Marta was away at a trade fair in Cologne. The team reviewed management targets, including a one euro deposit, a production cost under three euros per cup, and a goal of fifty partner cafes in the first year. They discussed initial design ideas, agreeing that the cup must be dishwasher-safe and fit standard takeaway lid sizes, while leaving a collapsible silicone design and app-based return tracking as open questions for now. Finally, Priya outlined homework assignments and scheduled the next meeting for functional design.
predictions.SY0110b: The team met for their second meeting to discuss functional design, reviewing materials, return processes, and feedback from Cologne cafe owners. They chose polypropylene for the cup material, agreeing on a stackable design with a ninety-millimetre rim, room for a logo, and a counter-return process without an app or return machines. The team also planned a dishwasher durability test at Café Lindner instead of the office kitchen.
predictions.SY0110c: The team reviewed the dishwasher test results for the polypropylene cups and agreed to use in-mould labelling for the logo, a ribbed band for grip, a single three hundred millilitre size, and a slate grey base colour. They also examined Jonas's counter return flow design, confirming a refund or direct swap option for customers, and approved the slate grey badge design with an enlarged logo. Finally, they assigned tasks for the upcoming detailed design meeting, including cost quotes, staff guidance, and management consultations.
predictions.SY0110d: The team held their final detailed design meeting while Jonas was absent due to illness, starting with a review of the moulding quote for ten thousand polypropylene cups at one euro fifty-four each. Tom confirmed the final cup specifications including the slate grey color, ribbed band, and embossed base text, while Marta reported that the one-page staff guide was well-received by a cafe owner and ready for lamination. Finally, the project manager reviewed the project against management requirements and assigned tasks for placing the order, laminating guides, and contacting cafes from the fair.
predictions.SY0202a: Project manager Marcus held a kickoff meeting with industrial designer Tomas, marketing expert Priya, and user interface designer Hannah to plan a new self-checkout kiosk for public libraries. The team discussed budget constraints, aiming for a production cost under four thousand euros per unit, and agreed that the kiosk should handle checkouts and renewals while leaving returns to existing book drops. They debated options for reading physical cards and digital phone apps, printed receipts, and touchscreen versus physical buttons, leaving several design details for further review. Priya agreed to gather library accessibility requirements during her user research, while Tomas and Hannah were assigned tasks regarding component layouts and user flows respectively, ahead of the next meeting.
predictions.SY0202b: The team met to discuss the functional design of the library kiosk, noting Hannah's absence due to illness. Industrial Designer reported on the current hardware setup, rough costs, and a casing design featuring wood panelling, while Marketing Expert shared user feedback prioritizing speed and accessibility requirements. The group agreed on email receipts with an optional print feature, lower shelf heights for wheelchair access, and a physical help button that also activates audio mode. Finally, they discussed barcode versus RFID options, leaving the final decision pending until pricing is confirmed.
predictions.SY0202c: The team held their third conceptual design meeting, reviewing RFID pricing, casing sketches, and the user flow. Priya presented RFID reader pad costs, leading the team to agree on using both an RFID pad and a barcode scanner fallback for the kiosk. Tomas shared three casing sketches, and the team selected the desk shape in oak veneer with aluminium corners to save money while keeping a furniture-like appearance. Hannah updated the user flow for RFID batch scanning, renewals, and the help button functions. The team decided to keep the fifteen-inch screen size for now and re-evaluate it after a physical mock-up.
predictions.SY0202d: The team held their final detailed design meeting, reviewing mock-ups, evaluation criteria, and costs in Hannah's absence. Tomas presented the foam-board mock-up, leading the team to settle on a seventeen-inch screen and a licensed board with a built-in text-to-speech engine to ensure quality for visually impaired users. Priya outlined her evaluation criteria, giving high scores across speed, accessibility, library look, print options, and staff help. Finally, the group calculated the unit cost at three thousand four hundred and ten euros, leaving them well under budget, and agreed on final action items before concluding the project design.
predictions.SY0209a: Laura opened the kickoff meeting for the new project to design a protective case for the Learnly seven-inch educational tablet targeted at children aged four to eight. The team discussed financial constraints, setting a twenty-five Euro selling price and a maximum twelve-fifty production cost, while confirming the case will be custom-fit for the Learnly tablet rather than universal. During brainstorming, they covered essential features such as drop protection using thick rubber or foam, a carrying handle, a raised lip to protect the screen, and a wipeable material for easy cleaning. Laura assigned tasks for the next meeting and announced that additional information from management would be sent by email.
predictions.SY0209b: The team met for their second functional design meeting, with Tomasz absent due to illness. They reviewed survey feedback about dropping and cleaning, agreed on a one-point-two metre drop target, and selected EVA foam as the main material. Priya outlined requirements for cut-outs, covered buttons, and a raised screen lip, while the group decided to use a fixed handle instead of a fold-out stand.
predictions.SY0209c: The team held a conceptual design meeting to review survey results, pricing, supplier quotes, and design features. Tomasz reported that survey respondents prioritized drop protection, cleaning, and handles, while teachers requested name tags and parents preferred bright, dirt-hiding colours. Ben presented a supplier quote of eight euros forty cents per case, with an additional thirty cents for a second colour, while Priya shared her handle and cut-out sketches. The group agreed to include a shallow wedge on the back for standing and a name tag window if it stays under a euro, selected strong blue and lime green as the launch colours, and decided to check the legal regulations regarding children's toys.
predictions.SY0209d: The team met for their final detailed design meeting, reviewing cost estimates, design sketches, and evaluation criteria. They agreed on using a foam pocket with a clear film for the name tag window on the back of the case and confirmed the price and total cost estimates remain well within budget. Finally, they reviewed evaluation scores based on user survey responses and assigned remaining action items before concluding the project.
predictions.SY0304a: Hannah, Priya, and Tom held a kickoff meeting for a new campus parking availability display project requested by the university estates office. They discussed the project parameters, noting a tight manufacturing budget of four pounds per unit and a deadline for the first installations at the start of next term. The team agreed that target users will include staff, students, and visitors, and initial ideas for the display included showing both a clear number of free spaces and a color indicator. Finally, they assigned tasks for the next meeting next week, where Marcus will look into sensing options and outdoor casing, Priya will survey campus users, and Tom will sketch screen layouts.
predictions.SY0304b: The team met for a functional design meeting to review user research, sensing options, display layouts, and power requirements for the car park sign project. Marketing presented survey findings showing strong support for readable numbers, color-coded status, and concerns about visibility, while sensing options narrowed down to barrier counters with a nightly reset due to cost. The team agreed on a sixty-centimetre LED sign displaying the car park name with agreed color thresholds and powered via the barrier mains supply, bringing total costs within budget.
predictions.SY0304c: The team discussed the conceptual design for the car park sign project, noting that the central sign near the main gate lacks a separate budget and is postponed. Tom presented a sixty-centimetre layout in navy, and feedback from Priya's open day suggested adding a P symbol and dropping the flashing warning due to safety concerns. The team reviewed power options, noting that the library car park lacks a mains supply and requires further investigation for electrical costs and wall mounting. Finally, the group confirmed the budget remains tight at around three hundred ninety pounds per sign, and assigned tasks for the upcoming detailed design phase.
predictions.SY0304d: The team held their final detailed design meeting for the car park sign project. They agreed that estates will cover the library car park electrical supply from their maintenance budget, and finalized mounting decisions with posts for the four surface car parks and a wall bracket for the library. The project manager reviewed Tom's layout, confirming the design features, color-coded LED numbers, and the required print files. They finalized the total costs per sign, keeping them just under the four hundred pound budget, and addressed potential counter drift by planning spot counts. Finally, they evaluated the design against survey feedback, agreeing it meets the brief while deferring the app and QR codes, and assigned remaining action items before concluding.
